case.title: QA report case
case.raw_input: URGENT! SBI KYC http://sbi-kyc-verify.in pay kyc.support@fakebank

analyses.input: URGENT! SBI KYC http://sbi-kyc-verify.in pay kyc.support@fakebank

rules.name: Urgency language
rules.explanation: Time pressure suppresses deliberation. These phrases demand action before the recipient can verify the claim.

rules.name: Financial / government impersonation
evidence: link does not belong to SBI: sbi-kyc-verify.in (official: sbi.co.in)
rules.explanation: A regulated brand is named while the message links to a domain the brand does not own. A brand name alone is not evidence; the mismatch is.

rules.name: Suspicious domain structure
evidence: Brand used outside its official domain: "sbi" appears in sbi-kyc-verify.in/
Typosquat / brand-combination domain: registrable label "sbi-kyc-verify" imitates "sbi"
rules.explanation: The linked domain independently fails structural checks in the URL engine (brand mismatch, TLD, typosquat or obfuscation).

rules.name: Insecure HTTP link
rules.explanation: Any credential or payment page served over plain HTTP is unsafe regardless of how it looks.

rules.name: Payment request / identifier
rules.explanation: The message routes the recipient toward a payment instrument — a UPI ID, wallet or bank account.

rules.name: Credential / OTP harvesting
rules.explanation: The message asks for an OTP, PIN, CVV or identity document, or pairs a document name with an action verb.

rules.name: URL shortener obfuscation
rules.explanation: A shortener prevents the recipient from seeing the destination before clicking.

rules.name: KYC / verification lure
rules.explanation: KYC and re-verification are the most common pretexts for Indian banking fraud.

rules.name: Authority / threat pressure
rules.explanation: Threats of arrest, FIR or legal action create fear that short-circuits verification.

rules.name: Reward / lottery lure
rules.explanation: Unexpected winnings, refunds or cashback are used to pull the recipient into a payment flow.

rules.name: APK / app install request
rules.explanation: A link to an Android package installs code outside the Play Store, where banking trojans are distributed.

rules.name: Family impersonation (new number)
rules.explanation: A "new number" or lost-phone story is paired with a request for money. Both halves are required: family words alone are common, and the combination is the scam.

rules.name: Fake job / task scam
rules.explanation: A work-from-home or part-time task offer is paired with daily earning claims. Legitimate employers do not recruit or pay through messaging apps.

rules.name: Accidental code / OTP forward request
rules.explanation: The sender claims a verification code was sent to you by mistake and asks you to forward it. No legitimate service asks you to pass on a code.

rules.name: Utility disconnection threat
rules.explanation: An electricity, gas, water or SIM disconnection is threatened with a payment link. Utilities do not disconnect over a texted link.

heuristics.name: Deep subdomain nesting
heuristics.explanation: Four or more subdomain levels are commonly used to bury a recognisable brand deep inside a long host.

heuristics.name: Brand used outside its official domain
evidence: official domains: sbi.co.in, onlinesbi.sbi, sbiyono.sbi, sbicard.com
heuristics.explanation: A protected brand appears in the host or path, but the registrable domain is not owned by that brand.

heuristics.name: Confusable skeleton matches a trusted name
heuristics.explanation: After Unicode confusable folding, the registrable label reads as a protected brand or popular domain that this host does not own.

heuristics.name: Mixed-script homoglyph hostname
heuristics.explanation: One label mixes Latin with Cyrillic or Greek letters that render identically — the classic homoglyph attack.

heuristics.name: Random-looking domain label
heuristics.explanation: Machine-generated labels lack normal vowel structure or mix in digits, which is typical of bulk phishing registration.

heuristics.name: Lure-word stuffing in hostname
heuristics.explanation: Three or more security or payment words packed into the hostname is a template signature, not a brand name.

heuristics.name: Another domain embedded in the host
heuristics.explanation: The host spells out a trusted domain inside its own name (paypal.com.evil.xyz); the real owner is the last labels.

heuristics.name: Trusted name reused on a different TLD
heuristics.explanation: Reusing a well-known second-level name on a cheap or unfamiliar TLD is a common look-alike strategy.

heuristics.name: Hyphen-stacked hostname
heuristics.explanation: Scam domains chain descriptive words with hyphens to look official (e.g. secure-login-verify).

heuristics.name: Numeric padding in hostname
heuristics.explanation: Digits in the registrable label are often used to mint look-alike domains at scale.

heuristics.name: Punycode or homoglyph hostname
heuristics.explanation: Internationalised or punycode characters can render as a different Latin brand name (homoglyph attack).

heuristics.name: High-abuse TLD
heuristics.explanation: This top-level domain is cheap, lightly policed and over-represented in phishing campaigns.

heuristics.name: Raw IP address instead of a domain
heuristics.explanation: Legitimate consumer services rarely publish links to a bare IP address.

heuristics.name: Non-standard network port
heuristics.explanation: Ports other than 80/443 bypass common URL filters and are unusual for public services.

heuristics.name: Unencrypted HTTP transport
heuristics.explanation: Credentials submitted over plain HTTP can be read or modified in transit.

heuristics.name: Script or data URL scheme
heuristics.explanation: A javascript:, data: or file: link does not point to a website; it runs or embeds content in the browser context.

heuristics.name: Userinfo obfuscation (@ in URL)
heuristics.explanation: Everything before @ is userinfo; browsers ignore it, so the real destination hides after the @.

heuristics.name: Unusually long URL
heuristics.explanation: Long URLs push the real destination out of view in mobile address bars and chat previews.

heuristics.name: Credential-harvesting path words
heuristics.explanation: Paths named for login, KYC or refund flows indicate a credential or payment capture page.

heuristics.name: URL shortener
heuristics.explanation: Shorteners hide the final destination until the link is opened.

heuristics.name: Encoded path obfuscation
heuristics.explanation: Heavy or double encoding hides the real path from filters and from the person reading the link.

heuristics.name: Listed on local blocklist
heuristics.explanation: The domain appears in a locally imported phishing blocklist snapshot.

heuristics.name: High-entropy domain label
heuristics.explanation: Randomly generated labels indicate automated phishing-domain registration.

heuristics.name: Typosquat / brand-combination domain
heuristics.explanation: The registrable domain is a look-alike of SBI; the brand does not own it.

evidence: official domains: sbi.co.in, onlinesbi.sbi, sbiyono.sbi, sbicard.com

result_json.summary: This message is a high-risk artefact. It triggers 6 rules for a combined weight of 95 (capped at 100). The strongest signals are financial / government impersonation (25), suspicious domain structure (25), urgency language (15). It invokes SBI while directing the recipient to sbi-kyc-verify.in, which is not an official SBI domain (sbi.co.in). Payment is redirected to kyc.support@fakebank, which uses an unregistered UPI handle — no regulated PSP issues it. Do not open the link. Preserve the message and report it to 1930 (national cybercrime helpline).
result_json.safetyAdvice: Never share OTPs, PINs or card details. Open your bank's official app to check KYC status instead of tapping links.
